question: A case of Fuch's dystrophy, asking which of the following is true?

options.C: If thickness of stroma increased more than 10%, patient will develop corneal edema.

explanation: - A is wrong because it is more in post-menopausal women o The classic history for Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy is a patient, more commonly a woman, in the fourth to fifth decade of life, with symptoms of reduced or fluctuating vision, glare, or in some cases recurrent foreign body sensation. o Patients classically experience morning blurry vision, as evaporation at the corneal surface is unable to occur overnight with eyelids closed, and the cornea swells during the night. Patients may have a family history of a corneal transplantation in one or more family members. - B is wrong because Fuchs' dystrophy is often inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. - C is closest to be true although I didn't find any source with this statement o The most common signs of Fuchs' Dystrophy include: Guttata on Descemet's membrane: the guttata tend to be central and slowly become more prominent peripherally Stromal edema; Endothelial folds; Epithelial microcysts, Epithelial bullae, Sub-epithelial fibrosis; Stromal haze and scar formation; Vascular ingrowth into the cornea

review.explanation: Fuchs endothelial dystrophy has a clear female preponderance, on the order of three to one, so the statement that males equal females is false. The common late-onset form is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance rather than recessive, with a TCF4 trinucleotide repeat expansion as the major risk allele, so that option fails too. By elimination the remaining statement stands: once endothelial pump failure lets the stroma thicken appreciably above baseline pachymetry the cornea decompensates and clinical oedema appears, which is why the patient describes vision that is worst on waking.
review.concern: The specific figure of 10 percent stromal thickening is not a standard published threshold; treat it as exam wording rather than a quotable number. A and B are definitively wrong, so C is the key by elimination.

question: What is the cause of a shield ulcer?
explanation: - In VKC: the allergic entity typically occurs in children within the first 2 decades of life during the spring or fall. - Classic ocular signs include: (1) giant papillary conjunctivitis; (2) "Horner- Trantas dots" which are jellylike limbal nodules representing degenerated eosinophils; and a (3) "shield ulcer" which is a corneal epithelial defect involving the upper half of the cornea. - The palpebral form of vernal has giant papillae. - The limbal form of vernal has Horner- Trantas dots. - Mast cell stabilizers take at least 2 weeks to reach effect. - The exact cause of shield ulcer in VKC is not fully understood, but it is believed to be related to the mechanical trauma caused by the giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, which rub against the cornea and damage the epithelium. - Another possible cause is the toxic effect of the inflammatory mediators and enzymes released by the eosinophils and mast cells that infiltrate the cornea in VKC. - A third possible cause is the secondary infection by bacteria or fungi that can colonize the ulcerated area and worsen the inflammation. - According to AAO2023: Corneal epithelial damage resulting from constant rubbing by superior tarsal giant papillae and cytotoxic agents secreted by eosinophils (major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein) may lead to the formation of oval-shaped noninfectious ulcers, so-called shield ulcers, in the superior or central cornea.

review.explanation: The vernal shield ulcer is a sterile oval epithelial defect in the upper cornea produced by mechanical abrasion from the giant tarsal papillae, compounded by the toxic effect of eosinophil major basic protein on the epithelium. Its plaque tends to resist re-epithelialization, which is why treatment combines intensive topical steroid with removal of the plaque and sometimes supratarsal steroid injection. Ordinary trauma produces a nonspecific abrasion without the giant papillae, Horner-Trantas dots and seasonal itching that define vernal keratoconjunctivitis.

question: A 38 yrs old presented with infiltrate near limbus associated with pain and photophobia, asking what is the diagnosis?
explanation: Although incomplete question with no pic and other choices - It could be infected pinguicula or PUK or marginal keratitis, but I think it is more toward phylectenular keratoconjunctivitis - Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is postulated to occur secondary to an allergic, hypersensitivity reaction at the cornea or conjunctiva, following re-exposure to an infectious antigen that the host has been previously sensitized to. - Antigens of Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are most commonly associated. - Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis may have an association with ocular rosacea, a skin condition that may have a similar underlying type IV hypersensitivity origin. Reference: Eyewiki

review.explanation: A painful photophobic infiltrate sitting near the limbus, typically with a clear interval between infiltrate and limbus, is the picture of marginal staphylococcal hypersensitivity keratitis or a phlyctenule, both of which are strongly associated with ocular rosacea and chronic blepharitis in this age group. Rheumatoid arthritis instead causes peripheral ulcerative keratitis, a crescentic melt with epithelial loss and stromal thinning right at the limbus, usually in long-standing seropositive disease and often with scleritis and systemic vasculitis.
review.concern: The recall is truncated with no image and only two options; the answer rests on the age and the description of a limbal infiltrate with pain and photophobia.

question: A case of MK (central ulcer with feathery margin), asking what is the best next step?
explanation: - This is a mycotic (fungal) keratitis not MK according to the mentioned features - In warmer climates the rule is that the most common organisms are filamentous fungi, like Fusarium spp and Aspergillus spp. with a strong relationship to trauma. - With filamentary fungi, the corneal lesions have a white/gray infiltrate with feathery borders. There might be satellite lesions with a hypopyon and conjunctival injection as well as purulent secretions. Ulcers caused by yeast are plaque-like and slightly more defined, similar to bacterial keratitis. - For a definitive diagnosis, scrapings taken from deep within the lesion should be made and inoculated in Sabouraud agar. The shortcoming is that it can take up to 3 weeks to grow and identify the organism. For a faster result, smears with special stains such as Gomori, PAS, acridine orange, calcofluor white or KOH should be performed. The drawback is that not all laboratories have these stains available, so, again we might need to rely on the patient's evolution and the physician's clinical acumen. If all labs and cultures are negative, corneal biopsy should be considered to obtain a specimen. - The following is my summary from the BSC2022 microbiology lecture: Reference: https://eyewiki.aao.org/Fungal_Keratitis BSC2022 lecture

review.explanation: A central ulcer with feathery indistinct margins, often with satellite lesions, an endothelial plaque or hypopyon, is filamentous fungal keratitis. Correct management is to scrape the base and edges of the ulcer for smears and culture, with KOH or calcofluor white and Giemsa plus Sabouraud medium, and to begin treatment at the same visit rather than waiting on the laboratory. Topical natamycin 5 percent is first-line for filamentous keratitis and performed better than voriconazole in the Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial, so treatment and sampling belong together. Antibacterial drops alone would leave the infection untreated.
review.concern: Option B contains everything option A contains plus the correct first-line drug, so B strictly dominates the source key. The only reading that makes A right is if the original stem asked specifically for the diagnostic step; withholding therapy from an infected cornea pending culture is not standard care.

question: After an attack of VZV 2 months ago, a patient presented complaining of redness, photophobia, decrease vision, and blurry vision of the same involved eye. The examination showed a disciform lesion with vascularization and an intact epithelial defect. What medication you would start the patient on?
explanation: - Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes both chickenpox (varicella) and shingles (herpes zoster). - After an episode of chickenpox, the virus travels in a retrograde manner to the dorsal root and cranial nerve sensory ganglia, where it may remain dormant for decades, with reactivation thought to occur after VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity has faded. - Vesicles involving the tip or side of the nose precede the development of ophthalmic herpes zoster (Hutchinson sign). - A prodromal phase precedes the appearance of the rash. It lasts 3-5 days and is characterized by tiredness, fever, malaise and headache. - Within 24 hours, groups of vesicles appear and these become confluent over 2-4 days. - The vesicles often pass through a pustular phase before they crust and dry after 2-3 weeks. - Acute epithelial keratitis develops in over 50% of patients within 2 days of the onset of the rash and usually resolves spontaneously within a few days. Dendritic lesions are smaller and finer than herpes simplex dendrites and have tapered ends without terminal bulbs - Nummular keratitis usually develops at the site of epithelial esions about 10 days after the onset of the rash. They are fine granular subepithelial deposits surrounded by a halo of stromal haze. - Stromal (interstitial) keratitis develops 3 weeks (in 5%) after the onset of the rash and significant scarring can occur. - Disciform keratitis (immune-mediated endotheliitis) is less common than with herpes simplex infection but may lead to corneal decompensation. Treatment is with topical steroids. Reference: - Kanski, Chapter 7, P227

review.explanation: Disciform stromal and endothelial keratitis after herpes zoster ophthalmicus is immune-mediated inflammation occurring with an intact epithelium, and it is treated with topical corticosteroid tapered slowly, generally with systemic antiviral cover. Trifluridine is a topical antiviral for herpes simplex epithelial disease, has no established role in varicella-zoster stromal keratitis, and is epitheliotoxic with prolonged use. The vascularization and the delayed presentation two months after the rash both fit chronic immune stromal disease rather than active viral epithelial replication.

question: A picture of a sup-nasal subluxated lens, asking what the effect of this is subluxated lens:
explanation: Another correct answer is astigmatism - A sublaxated lens can cause astigmatism or myopia depending on the degree and direction of the displacement. - A sublaxated lens can induce irregular astigmatism due to the tilt or decentration of the lens, which creates optical aberrations and changes the shape of the optical interfaces. - The power of the lens can be increased by osmotic changes, and changes in lens position or shape (anterior lens dislocation). - A sublaxated lens can also induce myopia if the lens moves forward or backward, which changes the effective power of the eye and shifts the focal point in front of the retina. Reference: Eyewiki

referenceLinks.title: Ectopia Lentis - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Definition of subluxation vs luxation, causes (Marfan, homocystinuria, trauma), and the refractive consequences - explicitly states that zonular disruption increases lens curvature and results in lenticular myopia and astigmatism

referenceLinks.title: File:Linsenluxation.png - Wikimedia Commons
referenceLinks.shows: Clinical photograph of a human displaced crystalline lens with ciliary/zonular fibres visible in the pupil (CC BY-SA 4.0)

figureFinding: Slit-lamp photo of a subluxated (partially dislocated) crystalline lens - the lens equator/edge visible crossing the pupil with stretched or broken zonules, here displaced supero-nasally.

review.explanation: When zonular support is lost the lens becomes more spherical and its power rises, and any forward shift increases the effective power of the eye, so the phakic portion of an eye with a subluxated lens is characteristically myopic, usually with marked and often irregular lenticular astigmatism. High hyperopia is what you measure through the aphakic portion of the pupil once the lens edge has moved out of the visual axis. Emmetropia would be a coincidence rather than an expected consequence.
review.concern: Astigmatism is an equally correct answer that was not offered; among the choices given, induced myopia is the standard teaching.

question: A Case of active Fuchs Heterochromic Iridocyclitis (Iris atrophy, mild cells, flares). The patient wants to do a cataract surgery, what you should discuss with the patient regarding the Post op complications?
explanation: - Fuchs uveitis syndrome (formerly Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis) is a relatively rare, insidious, and chronic form of uveitis that is typically unilateral. - There is no race or sex predilection, and it often manifests in young to middle adulthood. - It is characterized by iris heterochromia, low-grade anterior chamber inflammation, posterior subcapsular cataracts, and IOP elevation. The heterochromia is caused by loss of iris pigment in the affected eye, which is usually hypochromic in dark irides and hyperchromic in light irides. - The low-grade inflammation is often accompanied by small, stellate, pancorneal KPs. - Despite the low-grade inflammation, these patients are classically asymptomatic and present with a nonhyperemic eye. - Fuchs uveitis syndrome has variously been associated with toxoplasmosis, CMV, herpes simplex, and rubella - Secondary OAG occurs in approximately 15% of patients with this disease. - Gonioscopic examination reveals multiple fine vessels that cross the trabecular meshwork. These vessels are usually not accompanied by a fibrous membrane and typically do not result in PAS formation and secondary angle closure. - The vessels are fragile and may cause an anterior chamber hemorrhage, either spontaneously or resulting from trauma. A classic finding is anterior chamber hemorrhage after a paracentesis during intraocular surgery (Amsler sign). - Treatment of Fuchs uveitis syndrome is directed at controlling the IOP with topical ocular hypotensive medications. IOP control may be difficult, and the IOP does not necessarily correlate with the degree of inflammation. Corticosteroids are generally not effective in treating the low-grade chronic inflammation, and their use can elevate the IOP. Reference: AAO2023 Glaucoma P142

review.explanation: Fuchs uveitis syndrome features fragile abnormal angle vessels, and the classic surgical event is a filiform haemorrhage from the angle when the chamber is decompressed, the Amsler-Verrey sign, with hyphema the corresponding postoperative complication to warn the patient about. Postoperative inflammation in Fuchs is characteristically mild and these eyes generally do very well after phacoemulsification with a good visual outcome, so that is the weaker warning. Zonular laxity is a feature of pseudoexfoliation rather than of Fuchs uveitis; the other genuine long-term concern is secondary glaucoma.

question: What do JIA present with?
explanation: The signs of inflammation include fine KPs, band keratopathy, flare and cells, posterior synechiae, and cataract. Reference: AAO2023 Uveitis P142

review.explanation: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes a chronic non-granulomatous anterior uveitis in a white, quiet eye, classically in ANA-positive girls with oligoarticular disease, and the sequelae that define it are posterior synechiae, band keratopathy, cataract and secondary glaucoma. Because the eye is not red and the child is asymptomatic, screening slit-lamp examination is what detects it. Hypopyon points to HLA-B27-associated or Behcet uveitis, mutton-fat keratic precipitates to granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis or tuberculosis, and retinal vasculitis is not part of the JIA picture.

question: A patient presented with bilateral recurrent conjunctivitis follicular and urethritis, asking what is the treatment?
explanation: - Follicular conjunctivitis? This is not related to reactive arthritis which I believe it is the diagnosis. - Reactive arthritis may be considered in any case of chronic, nonfollicular, mucopurulent conjunctivitis with negative culture results. - Reactive arthritis (formerly called Reiter syndrome) is a systemic disorder characterized by the classic triad of ocular (conjunctivitis/episcleritis, iridocyclitis, or keratitis), urethral, and joint inflammation. - The most common ocular finding in reactive arthritis is a bilateral papillary conjunctivitis with mucopurulent discharge, which has been reported in 30%-60% - Look at this similar question from ophthaQ: Reference: AAO2023, P37 Oculo

review.explanation: Bilateral recurrent follicular conjunctivitis together with urethritis in a sexually active adult is adult inclusion conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K, in which the conjunctivitis is chronic and follicular with a stringy discharge and often a superior micropannus. Treatment must be systemic to clear the genital reservoir: a macrolide, azithromycin 1 gram orally as a single dose, or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for a week, with partner treatment and screening for other sexually transmitted infections. Topical therapy alone does not eradicate the organism and the infection recurs.
review.concern: Intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone treats gonococcal conjunctivitis, which is hyperacute and copiously purulent with marked chemosis and lid oedema, not follicular. The source explanation abandons the follicular finding to argue reactive arthritis, but reactive arthritis conjunctivitis is papillary and mucopurulent and is not treated with ceftriaxone either. Empiric ceftriaxone is often added for possible gonococcal co-infection, but the answer to this stem is the oral macrolide.

question: Which of the following is a contraindication of a laser trabeculoplasty ?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document. - In laser trabeculoplasty (LTP), laser energy is applied to the trabecular meshwork in discrete spots, usually covering 180°-360° per treatment. The goal of LTP is to reduce IOP by increasing outflow facility. - LTP is indicated to lower IOP in patients with: open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

review.explanation: Laser trabeculoplasty is contraindicated in angle-recession glaucoma, where the damaged meshwork responds poorly and pressure may rise after treatment; uveitic and neovascular glaucoma and ICE syndrome are in the same group. Open-angle glaucoma, including normal-tension glaucoma, and ocular hypertension are the indications for trabeculoplasty, not contraindications. Pigmentary glaucoma actually responds well, although lower energy is used because the heavily pigmented meshwork absorbs more energy and is prone to a post-laser spike.

question: Which of the following is highly suggestive of glaucoma daily variation?
explanation: Reference: OphthoQ

review.explanation: Physiological diurnal variation in intraocular pressure is roughly 2 to 6 mmHg, so a swing of 10 mmHg or more is abnormal and is characteristic of glaucomatous eyes, and it can explain progression in a patient whose office readings always look acceptable. A 4 to 6 mmHg range is within normal limits, and a single baseline of 22 mmHg is only marginally raised and says nothing about variation. A peak in the early morning hours is normal physiology, since IOP is typically highest around the end of the sleep period.

question: Picture showing inadvertent superior bleb, with shallow AC, low IOP, what would you do next?
explanation: - It looks like bleb leak although nothing mentioned if the pt has symptoms of excessive tearing or now and the bleb elevation. - Bleb leaks can occur at any point in the postoperative course. - In the early postoperative period, leaks most commonly occur at the incision site. - Unrecognized buttonholes and flap suture erosion through the conjunctiva can also lead to leaks. - They are often symptomatic (patients report experiencing excessive tearing) and can be found by performing a Seidel test. - In addition to hypotony, patients with a leak may have a shallow or normal anterior chamber depth and a low-lying bleb. - Untreated leaks can lead to early bleb fibrosis and infection. See this algorithm: Reference: AAO 2023 - Glaucoma P265

review.explanation: Hypotony with a shallow chamber in an eye with a filtering bleb requires you first to establish whether aqueous is escaping through the conjunctiva, and the Seidel test answers that at the slit lamp within seconds and at no cost. Only if it is negative do you go on to look for over-filtration or choroidal detachment, with B-scan if the view is poor. Finding a leak changes management immediately, to reduced steroid, aqueous suppression, a bandage contact lens, glue, suture or revision.

question: A case of a diabetic patient with ketoacidosis, asking what is the effect of IOP during the ketoacidosis phase?
explanation: - both by DKA itself or DKA as a result of treatment by glycerin - This diagram adopted from ophthaQ Reference: Eyewiki + ophthoQ

review.explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis combines marked hyperglycaemia and raised plasma osmolarity with dehydration and systemic acidosis, all of which reduce aqueous production and osmotically draw fluid out of the eye, so intraocular pressure falls during the acute phase. The clinically useful corollary is that pressure can rise during correction, if plasma osmolarity is brought down faster than intraocular osmolarity, and the same reverse-osmotic principle explains rebound after systemic glycerol or mannitol.

question: A case of a pregnant woman (Gestational Age: 8 weeks) who is known to have glaucoma, asking which of the following medications is safe for her to use?
explanation: All glaucoma medications are FDA class C (except for brimonidine and dipivefrin which are class B). However, nursing mothers should not given brimonidine or timolol since these are concentrated in the breast milk and can have severe adverse effects on the child. Reference: OphthoQ

review.explanation: Brimonidine is the only commonly used topical glaucoma agent in the old FDA pregnancy category B; timolol, the carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and the prostaglandin analogues are all category C, and prostaglandins are additionally avoided for their theoretical uterotonic effect. The essential caveat is that brimonidine must be stopped before delivery and during breastfeeding, because it crosses into breast milk and can cause CNS depression and apnoea in an infant, at which point timolol with punctal occlusion, or laser trabeculoplasty, become preferable. All topical therapy in pregnancy should be given with punctal occlusion and the lowest effective dose.

question: A picture of follicular reaction of upper tarsus, asking what medication causes this picture exclusively?
explanation: Reference: AAO: Cornea: CHAPTER 4: Conditions Associated With Ocular Surface Disorders, P103

review.explanation: Chronic follicular conjunctivitis of the upper tarsus is the classic toxic and delayed-hypersensitivity response to long-term topical medication, and among glaucoma drops the miotics, pilocarpine in particular, are the traditional culprits; pilocarpine is also implicated in drug-induced cicatricial pemphigoid with fornix shortening. Latanoprost typically causes conjunctival hyperaemia, lash growth and iris and periocular pigmentation rather than follicles. Timolol produces surface toxicity and dry eye plus systemic beta-blockade, and ceftriaxone is a systemic drug in this list.
review.concern: The word exclusively overstates the case, since brimonidine, apraclonidine, dipivefrin and topical antivirals also cause follicular conjunctivitis; among the options offered, pilocarpine is the answer.

question: A case of a patient who presented with high IOP and who is S/P office procedure. B-scan showed (may be exudative RD, or choroidal detachment), asking which of the following procedures you think is the cause?
explanation: - Adverse effects of scatter PRP include choroidal detachment as well as decreases in night vision, color vision, contrast sensitivity, peripheral vision, and, in rare cases, pupillary dilation. Some patients may experience a transient loss of 1 or 2 lines of visual acuity or increased glare following treatment. Other transient adverse effects include loss of accommodation, loss of corneal sensitivity, and photopsias. Macular edema may also be precipitated or worsened by PRP. Reference: AAO 2022 - P106 Retina and Vitreous

review.explanation: Extensive panretinal photocoagulation, especially delivered in one heavy session, causes choroidal effusion and exudative detachment with anterior rotation of the ciliary body, which shallows the chamber and closes the angle without pupillary block, producing high pressure with choroidal elevation on B-scan. It is managed with cycloplegia and topical steroid, and specifically not with miotics or a peripheral iridotomy. YAG capsulotomy raises pressure by liberating debris into the trabecular meshwork and intravitreal injection causes a transient volume-related spike, but neither produces choroidal detachment.

question: What device would you use to measure the IOP in a supine position?
explanation: I believe it is an except question as both Perkins and Pneumo "can be" used in supine position), If it is not "except" question and Schiøtz tonometry is choice D then I would choose it because it is the only one that is used only while the patient is supine. If it is not except question and Schiøtz not in the choices I will choose Perkins) - The Perkins tonometer is a portable Goldmann applanation tonometer that can be used with the patient in either the upright or supine positions - Pneumatonometer can be used with the patient in sitting, lateral decubitus, or supine body positions. - Although Schiøtz tonometry is now rarely used in the developed world, it remains the only form of tonometry that does not require electrical power. - Schiøtz tonometry determines IOP by measuring the amount of corneal indentation produced by a known weight. Measurements are taken with the patient supine. - Look at this table that I made by chatGPT using information in eyewiki: Reference: https://www.aao.org/education/bcscsnippetdetail.aspx?id=eaf2d8dd-ed51-4d1c-

review.explanation: Goldmann applanation tonometry is mounted on the slit lamp and can only be performed with the patient sitting upright, which is precisely why the portable Perkins tonometer exists: it applies the identical Goldmann principle in a hand-held instrument and works with the patient upright or supine, in theatre or at the bedside. The pneumatonometer likewise works sitting, supine or in lateral decubitus. Schiotz indentation tonometry, the one device used only supine, is not among the options.

Note however that two of the three options work supine, which is a hallmark of a mis-recalled all-except stem; if the original asked which device could NOT be used supine, the source key B would be correct. Treat this as a flawed recall and learn the instrument facts.

question: A glaucoma patient did a visual field, and he sees only central vision, which visual felid would you order to have more accurate results:
explanation: - For patients with advanced visual field loss or with paracentral defects, testing of the central field with the 10-2 or C8 pattern is appropriate. Reference: AAO

review.explanation: When the field is reduced to a small central island, the 24-2 pattern samples on a 6 degree grid and puts only a handful of points inside the central 10 degrees, so real change in the remaining vision is easily missed. The 10-2 places 68 points on a 2 degree grid within the central 10 degrees and tracks that residual island far more sensitively; it is also the pattern of choice for paracentral defects. Enlarging the stimulus to Goldmann size V helps further once defects are deep and the patient is near the floor of the instrument.

question: In hyperopic anisometropia, what is minimum amblyogenic anisometropia refractive error?
explanation: closest answer - Anisometropic amblyopia, dissimilar refractive errors in the 2 eyes cause 1 retinal image to be chronically defocused. - Levels of anisometropia that commonly lead to amblyopia are greater than 1.50 diopters (D) of anisohyperopia, 2.00 D of anisoastigmatism, and 3.00 D of anisomyopia. - See this table: Reference: AAO2023, pediatric, P58

review.explanation: In anisometropic amblyopia the more hyperopic eye is chronically defocused because the child accommodates for the better eye, and hyperopic anisometropia is the most amblyogenic type because that defocus is never relieved. The thresholds usually taught are roughly 1.00 to 1.50 dioptres of anisohyperopia, about 1.50 to 2.00 dioptres of anisoastigmatism and about 3.00 dioptres of anisomyopia. Of the numbers offered, 1.25 is the only one lying in that low range, since 0.50 dioptre is clinically insignificant and 2.00 and 5.00 dioptres are well above the minimum.
review.concern: BCSC most often quotes greater than 1.50 dioptres for anisohyperopia, so an examiner working from that figure could have intended 2.00. The choice hinges on whether minimum amblyogenic means the lowest level capable of causing amblyopia, which fits 1.25, or the published screening referral threshold.

question: A patient with hyperopia wearing plus glasses having squint, what do you think the measured angle would be:

options.A: The measured angle will be less than the true with glasses.
options.B: The measured angle will be more than the true with glasses.

explanation: - Because of uncorrected hyperopia, the patient must accommodate to focus the retinal image. Accommodation is accompanied by the other components of the near reflex, namely convergence and miosis. If the patient's fusional divergence mechanism is insufficient to compensate for the increased convergence tonus, esotropia results. The angle of esotropia is approximately the same at distance and near fixation and is generally between 20Δ and 30Δ. Patients with refractive accommodative esotropia have an average of +4.00 diopters (D) of hyperopia. - This child has residual (albeit less) esotropia after full correction of his hyperopia. This situation describes "partially accommodative esotropia." In this situation, surgery can be undertaken to correct the residual ET. However, parents must be warned that the goal of surgery is NOT to get the child out of glasses. Actually, these children will still need glasses to maintain orthotropia. - artially accommodative esotropia is similar to accommodative esotropia in that a significant component of the esotropia results from accommodative convergence. However, unlike pure accommodative esotropia, patients with partially accommodative esotropia show a reduction in the angle of esotropia when wearing glasses but have a residual esotropia despite provision of the full hyperopic correction. Reference: AAO2023, Pediatric, P96

review.explanation: A plus lens induces prism whose base points toward the optical centre, so a deviating eye looking through a peripheral part of its own hyperopic correction receives a prismatic effect that partially neutralizes the deviation. The result is that the angle measured through the glasses is smaller than the true angle, and the discrepancy grows with lens power and with the size of the deviation; minus lenses in a myope have the opposite effect and exaggerate the measurement. This matters when planning surgery on a high hyperope with accommodative esotropia, where the measurement must be interpreted with that bias in mind.

question: A child presented with a unilateral proptosis, feverish, CBC showed eosinophilia, what is the diagnosis
explanation: - I think this question is the same as what had in the Part I exam; here is the question:

review.explanation: Idiopathic orbital inflammation, or orbital pseudotumour, in a child presents as acute painful proptosis and is one of the few orbital conditions accompanied by peripheral eosinophilia, along with fever and malaise; it responds dramatically to systemic corticosteroids, which is itself diagnostically useful. Bacterial orbital cellulitis instead produces a neutrophil leucocytosis and is nearly always accompanied by ethmoid sinus disease on imaging. Paediatric orbital inflammation is more likely than the adult form to be bilateral and to be accompanied by uveitis or disc oedema.
review.concern: The image is unavailable; the eosinophilia is what distinguishes the two options here.

question: A picture for a child with: OD: XT on HT and poor vision (20\400) OS: (20\20) On left eye cover test, right eye is showing XT with no movement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: ? Maybe D I couldn't find any supporting resource, but it seems he has eccentric fixation as he is using a non-foveal point of the retina for fixation which resulted in poor visual acuity

review.explanation: The decisive finding is that covering the fixing left eye produces no movement of the right eye even though it looks exotropic, which means the right eye was already fixing and the exodeviation is apparent rather than real. That is pseudo-exotropia from a large positive angle kappa, and the classic cause is a dragged or ectopic macula, as seen after retinopathy of prematurity, familial exudative vitreoretinopathy or toxocara granuloma, which also explains poor acuity in that eye. A true sensory exotropia from optic atrophy would show a refixation movement when the fellow eye is covered.

question: Child after cylogel refraction had been agitated and feverish, what to do?

options.A: Reassure and observe for few hours

explanation: although other options are not written esp if mentioned supportive treatment would be more correct) For me it is A until proven otherwise. If developed during cyclo, discontinue the drug, with supportive measures as necessary (so stop it and give paracetamol).; Cycloplegic agents act by paralyzing the sphincter muscle of the iris, and thereby producing iris dilation, and by paralyzing the ciliary muscle, which inactivates accommodation.; Local allergic reactions to cycloplegic drugs may include conjunctivitis, edematous eyelids, and dermatitis.; Cycloplegic agents may also cause nonallergic systemic symptoms, which may be more common in children with lighter irides; these include fever, dry mouth, flushing, tachycardia, constipation, urinary retention, nausea, dizziness, and delirium.; The side effects of systemic absorption in children consist of rapid pulse, fever, flushing, and mouth dryness.; Treatment is discontinuation of the drug, with supportive measures as necessary; See the following similar question from last minutes optics:

review.explanation: Fever, flushing, dry mouth, tachycardia, agitation and even frank delirium are recognized systemic anticholinergic effects of cyclopentolate and atropine absorbed through the nasal mucosa, and they are self-limited. The right response is to stop further instillation, observe the child with reassurance, antipyretics and fluids, and use punctal occlusion and lower concentrations at future visits. Intravenous therapy, or physostigmine, is reserved for severe toxicity with cardiovascular or respiratory compromise, which this presentation is not.

question: Picture of aniridia. Patient has vision of 20/200 and IOP of 30 mmHg. What else he might have?
explanation: Aniridia is a disease marked by bilateral hypoplastic irides, foveal hypoplasia with poor visual acuity, and frequent nystagmus. Other associated common features include glaucoma, optic nerve hypoplasia, cataracts, and the development of diffuse corneal scarring later in life from limbal stem cell deficiency. The disease is caused by PAX6 gene mutations and can be hereditary or arise de novo. In those cases of hereditary aniridia there is no increased risk for Wilms tumor (also known as nephroblastoma) over the general population. In patients with seemingly sporadic aniridia, up to one third of patients will develop Wilms tumor and most are diagnosed with the tumor by 5 years of age. All children with sporadic aniridia should undergo genetic testing for the Wilms tumor genetic defect. Most patients with aniridia will have photosensitivity simply due to the large amount of light entering the eye. Reference: OphthoQ

review.explanation: PAX6-related aniridia is a panocular disorder in which the visible iris hypoplasia is only part of the picture: the poor acuity and nystagmus come from foveal hypoplasia, and optic nerve hypoplasia, cataract, glaucoma from progressive angle closure by the rudimentary iris stump, and late limbal stem cell deficiency with corneal scarring complete it. Blood in Schlemm canal signifies raised episcleral venous pressure, as in Sturge-Weber or a carotid-cavernous fistula, or hypotony, and is not a feature of aniridia. Remember that sporadic aniridia mandates genetic testing and renal surveillance for Wilms tumour.

question: A picture of a patient with XT at primary position, limited adduction of the right eye with up shooting, what's your diagnosis?
explanation: In Duane retraction syndrome (DRS) there is failure of innervation of the lateral rectus by a hypoplastic sixth nerve nucleus, with anomalous innervation of the lateral rectus by fibres from the third nerve. Why the answer is type 2? Because in type 1 (which is the most common), the patient has: Limited or absent abduction: Normal or mildly limited adduction. In the primary position, straight or slight esotropia. But type 2 (the least common), the patient will have: Limited adduction. Normal or mildly limited abduction. In primary position, straight or slight exotropia (see the attached picture) Why then he has an up-shoot or down-shoot in adduction? In some cases, this is produced by a tight lateral rectus muscle slipping over or under the globe to produce an anomalous vertical movement. What are the other DRS Clinical features? A face turn is typical and confers BSV with the face in the turned position, thus avoiding amblyopia. Complete or partial restriction of abduction. Restricted adduction, usually partial. Retraction of the globe on adduction as a result of cocontraction of the medial and lateral recti with resultant narrowing of the palpebral fissure. Deficiency of convergence in which the affected eye remains fixed in the primary position while the unaffected eye is converging. Reference: Kanski P735

review.explanation: Duane type 2 is the rare form with limited adduction, relatively preserved abduction and an exotropia in primary position, which is exactly what is described. The up-shoot in adduction is the leash phenomenon, produced by the tight co-contracting lateral rectus slipping over the globe, and it can occur in any Duane type, so it does not change the classification. Type 1, the commonest, has limited abduction with esotropia, and bilateral inferior oblique overaction would be bilateral, with a V pattern and otherwise full ductions.

question: A 38-year-old with chin up and a picture for a patient with right Brown syndrome. What is the highest diagnostic test?

options.C: Normal passive elevation test on abduction
options.D: Restricted passive elevation test on adduction

explanation: So in the question possibly there will be an attached picture showing straight eyes in primary position, but adduction and elevation gaze of the affected eye will be restricted. This is brown, and it is important to know that all types have limited elevation in adduction, and other features differ according to the severity. In mild cases: No hypotropia in primary position or down-shoot in adduction. In moderate cases: Down-shoot in adduction In sever cases: Down-shoot in adduction. Hypotropia in the primary position + Chin-up head posture + Face turn away from the affected eye (to avoid the hypotropia allows for binocular fusion and comfortable vision) A positive, forced duction test confirms the diagnosis. A 'V' pattern is said to be significant when the difference between upgaze and downgaze is ≥15 Δ. Note that brown syndrome can cause V pattern. An 'A' pattern is considered significant if the difference between upgaze and downgaze is ≥10 Δ. Reference: Kanski P738 X-linked retinoschisis is linked to mutations in the RS1 gene, which encodes retinoschisin, a protein secreted by photoreceptors and involved in intercellular adhesion and likely retinal cellular organization. On histopathological examination, the splitting in X-linked retinoschisis occurs predominantly in the nerve fiber layer.; Patients typically present at school age complaining of poor vision or difficulty in school; On fundoscopic examination, 98-100% of patients have foveal schisis, noted as a spoke wheel pattern radiating from the fovea and a domelike elevation of a thin

review.explanation: Brown syndrome is a mechanical restriction of the superior oblique tendon and trochlea complex, so the confirmatory test is a forced duction showing restricted passive elevation of the eye in adduction, with far freer elevation in abduction. That positive forced duction is what separates Brown syndrome from inferior oblique palsy, in which the same motility pattern is present but forced ductions are free. The V pattern and chin-up head posture are consequences of the restriction rather than diagnostic tests, and a normal passive elevation in abduction is expected in Brown syndrome and therefore proves nothing on its own.

question: Attached picture showing Duane Syndrome with overshooting, asking what is the appropriate surgical management of this patient?
explanation: In Duane syndrome: An up-shoot or down-shoot (leash phenomenon) in adduction may be present; this is produced by a tight lateral rectus muscle slipping over or under the globe to produce an anomalous vertical movement. Surgery cannot cure Duane Retraction Syndrome, but it can o correct for the deviation in the primary position, thereby improving a compensatory head position that can occur in some individuals. o improve the leash phenomenon Indications for Surgery (at least one of the following characteristics): o * an abnormal head position greater than or equal to 15 degrees o * a significant deviation in the primary position o * Severe induced ptosis: a reduction of greater than or equal to 50% of the width of the palpebral fissure on adduction See the surgical treatment options: Reference: https://eyewiki.aao.org/Duane_Retraction_Syndrome

review.explanation: The up-shoot or down-shoot in Duane syndrome is a leash phenomenon in which the tight, co-contracting lateral rectus slips above or below the globe on adduction. Y-splitting the lateral rectus, with or without recession, converts it into a broad sling that straddles the globe and cannot slip, which is the standard procedure for the overshoot. Splitting the medial rectus does not address the mechanism, and medial rectus recession treats the esotropia of type 1 rather than the shoots; resections are avoided in Duane because they worsen globe retraction and fissure narrowing.

question: Picture attached showing a boy with a chin-up posture, asking what could be the cause?
explanation: Answer A and B would have chin down posture - MED, brown syndrome, and A pattern esotropia have a chin up posture) - In monocular elevation deficiency: there is a profound inability to elevate one eye across the horizontal plane, from abduction to adduction (See pic) with Chin elevation may be present. - Know that indications for surgical treatment of monocular elevation deficiency include a large hypotropia on primary gaze and a chin-up head position. There are two main causes of monocular elevation deficiency: (1) Tight inferior rectus; and (2) Weak elevators of the eye (i.e. superior rectus / inferior oblique). This is why this condition used to be called double- elevator palsy. In strabismus surgery, one of the concepts is to release the restriction if there is a restriction. So we need to determine if the patient's monocular elevation deficiency is due to a tight inferior rectus or if it is due to weakly- innervated elevators. Thus, to differentiate the etiology, one would perform forced ductions. If there is restriction on forced ductions, then an inferior rectus; recession is appropriate. In the absence of restriction, one would transpose the medial and; lateral recti to the superior rectus. This is called the Knapp

review.explanation: Head postures follow the field of single binocular vision or of best alignment. In monocular elevation deficiency the eye cannot be raised across the whole upper field, the hypotropia is worst in upgaze, and the child lifts the chin so that the eyes rest in downgaze, where alignment is best; a chin-up posture is in fact one of the surgical indications together with a large primary-position hypotropia. V-pattern esotropia is least deviated in upgaze, so those children put the chin down, and A-pattern exotropia is likewise smallest in upgaze and gives a chin-down posture. The chin-up group is A-pattern esotropia, V-pattern exotropia, Brown syndrome and monocular elevation deficiency.

question: You are doing a retinoscopy for a myopic patient; how would you know if reached the neutralization point?
explanation: Reference: BSC Optometry (Objective Refraction Lecture), 2022

review.explanation: As you approach neutrality the retinoscopic reflex becomes wider, brighter and faster, until it fills the pupil and appears to flash on and off with no identifiable direction of movement. That endpoint is the same whatever the starting refractive error, because all you are doing is bringing the patient far point to your peephole, then subtracting the working distance. A narrow, slow, dim streak means you are still far from neutrality, and skew or oblique movement of the reflex indicates an obliquely oriented astigmatic axis that needs the streak realigned, not neutralization.

question: You are doing a retinoscopy for a hyperopic patient; how would you know if reached the neutralization point?
explanation: same as previous question Reference: BSC Optometry (Objective Refraction Lecture), 2022

review.explanation: The endpoint of retinoscopy is identical in a hyperope and a myope: a broad, bright reflex filling the pupil and moving so fast that no direction can be identified. The refractive error only determines whether the reflex initially moves with or against the streak, and therefore whether you add plus or minus to reach neutrality; a hyperope shows with movement and needs plus. Remember to subtract the working distance, for example 1.50 dioptres at 67 cm, once neutrality is reached.

question: A question with refraction given 4.00 + 1.25 x90 (K reading given: 44 D @ 90 and 42 D @ 180), asking what type of astigmatism is this?
explanation: - So you can solve this question by seeing the refraction or the K readings. - For the refraction make the cylinder positive (here is it is already positive) then look to the axis; since it is 90 so it is within the range of the WTR astigmatism (60 to 120). - For the K readings it is steepest (44 D) at the 90 axis, so it is WTA. Reference: AAO Self assessment Others

review.explanation: With-the-rule astigmatism means the steeper corneal meridian is the vertical one, and the keratometry given, 44 dioptres in the 90 degree meridian against 42 at 180, is exactly that. The refraction agrees: written in plus-cylinder form, an axis at or near 90, conventionally within about 60 to 120 degrees, is with-the-rule. Against-the-rule would be a plus cylinder at about 180, and oblique astigmatism sits near 45 or 135 degrees.

question: Which of the following fungi is non-septate?
explanation: Nonseptate filamentous fungi include Mucor, Absidia, and Rhizopus. These fungi can cause life- threatening infections ("mucormycosis") of the paranasal sinuses, brain, and orbit, typically in immunocompromised patients. Septate fungi include Fusarium, Aspergillus, and Curvularia. A nice mnemonic is: "F.A.C.t.S" Reference: OphthaQ

review.explanation: Mucor, with Rhizopus and Absidia, is the classic broad, non-septate, ribbon-like filamentous fungus that branches at right angles and causes rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis in ketoacidotic or immunosuppressed patients. Aspergillus, Fusarium and Curvularia are all septate; Fusarium is the leading cause of filamentous fungal keratitis in warm climates and after contact lens wear, and Aspergillus branches at acute angles of roughly 45 degrees.

question: Child his mother noticed that he got confused between green and red colors, and between … and Violet. what is his problem:
explanation: Colour vision depends on three populations of retinal cones, each with a specific peak sensitivity: blue (tritan) at 414-424 nm, green (deuteran) at 522-539 nm and red (protan) at 549-570 nm. Any given cone pigment may be deficient (e.g. protanomaly - red weakness) or entirely absent (e.g. protanopia - red blindness). Trichromats possess all three types of cones (although not necessarily functioning perfectly), while absence of one or two types of cones renders an individual a dichromat or monochromat, respectively. Those with red-green deficiency caused by abnormality of red-sensitive cones are protanomalous, those with abnormality of green-sensitive cones are deuteranomalous and those with blue-green deficiency caused by abnormality of blue- sensitive cones are tritanomalous. Achromatopsia is a group of congenital disorders in which colours cannot be perceived and visual acuity is reduced. In rod monochromatism (AR) visual acuity is poor, typically 6/60. There is congenital nystagmus and photophobia. Colour vision is totally absent, all colours appearing as shades of grey. Blue cone monochromatism (XLR) features only slightly sub- normal acuity at 6/6-6/9, but colour vision is completely absent. Reference: Kanski

review.explanation: Confusion spanning both the red-green and the blue-violet axes cannot be produced by loss of a single cone class, which is what defines a dichromat: a protanope confuses reds and greens, a tritanope confuses blues and violets, and each has one confusion axis only. Loss of all cone function, that is achromatopsia or rod monochromatism, produces confusion across every axis, and in a child it comes with reduced acuity, photophobia and nystagmus. Dichromacy is a category rather than a diagnosis and is in any case excluded by the two-axis confusion.
review.concern: One colour is missing from the recalled stem, and a congenital achromat usually comes to attention with nystagmus and poor vision rather than with colour confusions noticed by a parent, so the item is imperfect as recalled.

question: 4yrs Old with left head turn Since 3 yrs ago , when fixating by right eye the deviation is 15 PD and when fixating by left the deviation is 35 PD . wt is the dx ?
explanation: In Duane retraction syndrome (DRS) there is failure of innerva- tion of the lateral rectus by a hypoplastic sixth nerve nucleus, with anomalous innervation of the lateral rectus by fibres from the third nerve. The condition is often bilateral. Up to half of patients have associated systemic defects such as deafness, external ear abnormalities, speech disorder and skeletal abnormalities. Classification (Huber) Type I, the most common, is characterized by (Fig. 18.62): I. Limited or absent abduction. II. Normal or mildly limited adduction. III. In the primary position, straight or slight esotropia. Type II, the least common, is characterized by (Fig. 18.63): I. Limited adduction. II. Normal or mildly limited abduction. III. In primary position, straight or slight exotropia. Type III is characterized by: I. Limited adduction and abduction. II. In the primary position, straight or slight esotropia. III. In some cases phenotypic variants have been allied to differing genotypes. Reference: Kanski Cataract can be Caused by:

review.explanation: The deviation measured with the left eye fixating, 35 prism dioptres, exceeds that measured with the right eye fixating, 15 prism dioptres, and by Hering law the secondary deviation is the larger one, obtained when the restricted eye fixates, which localizes the problem to the left eye. A left face turn is the compensatory posture for a left abduction deficit, since it places the eyes in right gaze and allows fusion. Limited abduction with esotropia is Duane type 1, whereas a right Duane type 2 would give limited adduction with exotropia and the larger deviation on right eye fixation.

question: Best describe Cataract in narrow angle glaucoma:

options.C: Lens become more brown in Color

explanation: ? The mechanism of phacomorphic glaucoma is typically multifactorial. However, by definition, a significant component of the pathologic angle narrowing is related to the acquired mass effect of the cataractous lens itself. As seen in the primary angle-closure (PAC) spectrum, pupillary block often plays an important role in this condition. Phacomorphic narrowing of the angle generally occurs slowly with formation of the cataract. Posterior Capsular opacification stems from the continued viability of lens epithelial cells that remain after removal of the nucleus and cortex. Opaque secondary membranes are formed by proliferating lens epithelial cells, fibroblastic metaplasia, and collagen deposition. Reference: AAO Glaucoma and Lens sections lacrimal gland ducts drained in:

review.explanation: The lens change that actually produces angle narrowing is nuclear sclerosis: as the nucleus hardens it becomes thicker and brunescent (brown), pushing the lens-iris diaphragm forward, increasing iris-lens contact and pupillary block, and crowding the angle. This is the phacomorphic mechanism, so a lens that has become more brown in colour is the description that fits. Posterior subcapsular opacity is the pattern of steroid use, diabetes, uveitis and radiation, and it has no bearing on angle depth. Lens fibre metaplasia describes the fibroblastic change of lens epithelial cells behind an IOL (posterior capsule opacification), not a cataract that closes an angle.
review.concern: The recall is ambiguous. If the examiner meant the lens findings after an acute angle-closure attack, the expected answer would be glaukomflecken, which are grey-white anterior subcapsular opacities from focal lens epithelial necrosis, and option D would become tempting. The stem says narrow angle glaucoma rather than acute attack, so the phacomorphic reading is the better one.

question: 3 prism diopter base Out Over the right eye , what is equivalent to it:

options.A: 2 pd bi Od and 1 pd bi OS =3
options.B: 2 pd bO Od and 1 pd bi OS
options.C: 1.5 pd bO Od and 1.5 pd bi OS

explanation: The source also notes: Ideal answer= (BO OU 1.5 AND 1.5)

review.explanation: Prism splitting divides the total requirement equally between the two eyes in the same vergence direction, so 3 prism dioptres base out over the right eye is equivalent to 1.5 base out over each eye. Base out in one eye and base in in the fellow eye are not equivalent to each other: their bases point the same way in space, so they act as a yoked (version) prism and largely cancel in vergence terms rather than adding. That is why option B (2 base out right, 1 base in left) delivers a net vergence of only about 1 prism dioptre base out, and option A is 3 prism dioptres base in, the wrong direction entirely.
review.concern: I disagree with the keyed answer B. The source note itself states the ideal answer is 1.5 and 1.5 base out in both eyes, and option C is the only choice carrying the correct 1.5/1.5 split, so its bi OS is almost certainly a transcription error for bO OS. Read literally none of the three options is correct, so this item should be treated as a flawed recall; the principle to memorise is simply that prism is split equally and in the same base direction between the eyes.

explanation: The paradigm for HLA-B27-associated AAU is a young man with acute-onset unilateral ocular pain and photophobia with redness and visual blur. Visual acuity in the affected eye is usually somewhat (but not markedly) reduced. Ocular examination is characteristically difficult because of photophobia. There is marked ciliary injection and severe AAU with small keratic precipitates inferiorly, anterior chamber (AC) cells 2-4+, often with fibrinous coagulum inferiorly, and sometimes with an hypopyon. Fibrin may form a web within the AC, the aqueous humor may be plasmoid (full of leaked plasma proteins so that normal thermal flow is sluggish), and incipient posterior synechiae are common (Fig. 7.14.1). The intraocular pressure is reduced, usually less than 10 mm Hg. Reference: Yanoff and Duker

review.explanation: HLA-B27 associated acute anterior uveitis is characteristically explosive and intensely fibrinous, with 3 to 4 plus cells, fibrin web in the anterior chamber, rapid posterior synechiae and often a frank hypopyon, so a severe acute hypopyon uveitis is the classic picture. It is typically unilateral or alternating between eyes rather than simultaneously bilateral, which makes option A wrong. Option B is too absolute: retinal vasculitis and cystoid macular oedema are uncommon but recognised in the spondyloarthropathy group. Option D is also false because not all TNF inhibitors behave alike, etanercept being notably ineffective for uveitis and even associated with paradoxical new-onset uveitis, whereas the monoclonal antibodies infliximab and adalimumab work.

question: Topical anti glaucoma that aggravate pupil block in Chronic angle Closure
explanation: The effect of miotics is to pull the peripheral iris away from the anterior chamber angle. However, strong miotics may also cause the zonular fibers of the lens to relax, allowing the lens-iris interface to move forward. Furthermore, their use results in greater iris-lens contact, thus potentially increasing pupillary block. Reference: AAO glaucoma Section

review.explanation: Miotics such as pilocarpine constrict the sphincter and pull the peripheral iris out of the angle, which is why they help in acute attacks, but they also relax the zonule and allow the lens to move forward and thicken, and they increase the area of iris-lens contact. Both effects can worsen pupillary block and even precipitate a plateau or malignant configuration in a chronically narrow angle. Beta blockers, prostaglandin analogues and alpha agonists do not alter the iris-lens relationship in a way that increases block; alpha agonists such as brimonidine and apraclonidine cause mydriasis but not pupillary block, and prostaglandins are safe in angle closure once the angle has been opened.

question: what is the deposit in Schnyder dystrophy
explanation: Pathologically, the opacities are accumulations of unesterified and esterified cholesterol and phospholipids. Reference: AAO External disease Section

review.explanation: Schnyder corneal dystrophy is a disorder of local corneal lipid metabolism caused by UBIAD1 mutations, and the deposits are unesterified and esterified cholesterol together with phospholipids. Clinically this produces the central crystalline opacity, a dense arcus lipoides at an unusually young age and diffuse midperipheral stromal haze, and the patient should be screened for systemic hyperlipidaemia. Lipid plus glycoprotein does not describe it, and collagen accumulation is not the abnormality here; note that the crystals are absent in about half of cases, so the diagnosis rests on the arcus and stromal haze as much as on crystals.

question: what type of laser is used to Cauterize a Corneal neovascularization
explanation: Argon laser treatment with and without fluorescein, photodynamic therapy with verteporfin, and subconjunctival and topical bevacizumab have been reported to reduce corneal neo- vascularization and lipid deposition. Reference: AAO External disease and cornea Section

review.explanation: Argon laser photocoagulation, applied directly to the feeder vessels at the limbus, is the classically described method of occluding corneal neovascularisation, because the blue-green argon wavelengths are strongly absorbed by haemoglobin in the vessel lumen. Excimer is a 193 nm ablative ultraviolet laser used for photorefractive tissue removal and produces no thermal coagulation of vessels. Krypton red penetrates deeply and is poorly absorbed by haemoglobin, which is precisely why it is used to treat through blood and pigment rather than to close vessels. Adjunctive options in current practice include fine-needle diathermy, photodynamic therapy with verteporfin and topical or subconjunctival bevacizumab.
review.concern: A yellow 577 nm laser is also well absorbed by oxyhaemoglobin and has been used for vascular targets, so option D is not physically absurd; argon remains the answer described in the cornea literature for this indication.

question: True about Mittendorf dot
explanation: Mittendorf dot is a common anomaly observed in many healthy eyes. A small, dense white spot generally located inferonasal to the posterior pole of the lens, a Mittendorf dot is a remnant of the posterior pupillary membrane of the tunica vasculosa lentis Reference: AAO External disease and cornea Section

review.explanation: A Mittendorf dot is a small dense white opacity on the posterior lens capsule, characteristically just inferonasal to the posterior pole, marking the site where the hyaloid artery attached to the tunica vasculosa lentis. It is a benign, common, non-progressive incidental finding in otherwise healthy eyes, which rules out option B. Calling it persistent fetal vasculature is misleading, because that clinical diagnosis denotes a sight-threatening entity with a retrolental fibrovascular stalk, microphthalmos, leukocoria and elongated ciliary processes, whereas a Mittendorf dot alone needs no intervention.

explanation: Tears in the Tenon capsule with prolapse of orbital fat into the sub-Tenon space can cause formation of a fibrofatty scar that may restrict ocular motility. Surgery involv- ing the inferior oblique muscle is particularly prone to this complication because of the proximity of the fat space to the posterior border of the inferior oblique muscle. If recognized at the time of surgery, the prolapsed fat can be excised and the rent closed with absorbable sutures. Meticulous surgical technique usually prevents this serious complication. Reference: AAO pediatric Section After eom sx he has decrease in palpebral fissure which was not there before the sx

review.explanation: This is fat adherence syndrome. Violation of the posterior Tenon capsule allows orbital fat to prolapse into the sub-Tenon space, where it organises into a fibrofatty scar that tethers the globe and produces a restrictive limitation with a positive forced duction test. Inferior oblique surgery is particularly liable to this because the posterior border of the muscle sits immediately against the inferotemporal fat pad. Injury to the intermuscular septum or to the anterior Tenon capsule causes little functional restriction, and damage to the neurovascular bundle of the inferior oblique would produce a paretic underaction with a negative forced duction test, not a positive one.

question: Old age man with blind painful eye IOP 45, What to do next:
explanation: cyclodestructive procedures can be used in painful eyes with poor vision potential in an attempt to provide comfort by lowering the IOP. However, there is a small risk of sympathetic ophthalmia with cyclodestructive procedures; thus, eyes without light perception should be treated with caution. The combination of corticosteroid and cycloplegic therapy can be very ef- fective in controlling pain in such eyes. Reference: AAO Glaucoma Section

review.explanation: In a blind painful eye the goal is comfort, and the first step is medical: a topical cycloplegic such as atropine combined with a topical corticosteroid controls the ciliary spasm and inflammation that generate most of the pain, and aqueous suppressants can be added for the pressure. Cyclodestruction is reserved for eyes that remain painful despite this, and it carries a small but real risk of sympathetic ophthalmia, so it is used cautiously in eyes with no light perception. A tube shunt is illogical here because there is no vision to preserve and it exposes a blind eye to the risks of intraocular surgery.
review.concern: Diode cyclophotocoagulation is a perfectly appropriate second step if the cycloplegic and steroid regimen fails to relieve pain, so option B is not wrong in principle, only wrong as the immediate next move.

explanation: An unequivocally positive forced duction test demonstrating restricted passive el- evation in adduction is essential for the diagnosis. Retropulsion of the globe during this test stretches the superior oblique tendon and accentuates the restriction. In restrictions involving the inferior rectus muscle or its surrounding tissues, by contrast, the limitation of passive elevation is accentuated by forceps-induced proptosis of the eye rather than by retropulsion. Attempts at elevation straight upward usually cause divergence (V pattern) due to lateral diversion of the globe as it meets resistance from the tight superior oblique tendon (see Fig 12-5). This finding is an important point of distinction from inferior oblique muscle paralysis, which is more likely to exhibit an A pattern. In adduction, the palpebral fissure widens and overdepression in adduction can be observed in severe cases of Brown syndrome (see Chapter 11, Table 11-2). This differs from overdepression in adduction in true superior oblique muscle overaction, which occurs less abruptly with increasing ad- duction. In mild Brown syndrome, no hypotropia is present in primary position. Severe cases of Brown syndrome with a primary position hypotropia are often accompanied by a chin-up head position or a head turn away from the side of the affected eye. review.explanation: Brown syndrome is a mechanical restriction of the superior oblique tendon-trochlea complex, so the single most diagnostic test is a forced duction demonstrating restricted passive elevation in adduction, accentuated by retropulsing the globe which tightens the tendon. Options A and B describe pattern strabismus: a V pattern can accompany Brown syndrome because the eye diverges as it meets the tight tendon on attempted upgaze, but a pattern is a supporting sign rather than a diagnostic test, and an A pattern points instead towards inferior oblique palsy. A normal passive elevation in abduction is expected in Brown syndrome but is not itself diagnostic, since it merely confirms the restriction is position-dependent.

explanation: ? Asthenopic symptoms include fatigue, headache, "eyestrain," double vision, fluctuating visual acuity, and lengthening of the clearest reading distance. They suggest hyperopic refractive errors, presbyopia, "accommodative spasm," or the possibility that the patient's existing glasses contain a stronger myopic correction (or a weaker hyperopic correction) than is necessary. review.explanation: Distortion is the optical signature of cylindrical correction, because a cylinder magnifies differentially along one meridian and so tilts or slants straight lines and floors, an effect that is worst with oblique axes and with newly prescribed or changed cylinder. Plus lenses additionally produce pincushion distortion from prismatic effect increasing toward the lens periphery. The accompanying asthenopia comes from the patient trying to fuse and adapt to that meridional magnification. Vertex distance changes the effective power of a strong lens rather than producing distortion per se, and crowding is a psychophysical amblyopia phenomenon with nothing to do with lens optics.

question: Calcification in RB :
explanation: Calcification within retinoblastoma is dystrophic and occurs within regions of necrosis. Intralesional calcification is found with other cancers including malignancies of the breast, prostate, and lung. In children, both neuroblastoma and Wilms tumor can display intralesional calcification. 0can%20display%20intralesional%20calcification. Reference: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaophthalmology/fullarticle/422488#:~:t ext=Calcification%20within%20retinoblastoma%20is%20dystrophic,tumor%2

review.explanation: Retinoblastoma outgrows its blood supply, and the ischaemic tumour beyond the viable perivascular cuffs undergoes necrosis; calcium is then deposited into that dead tissue, which is dystrophic calcification. This is why calcification is the single most useful ultrasound and CT sign in a paediatric leukocoria workup. It is not a consequence of haemorrhage, and it does not arise from metaplasia of the retinal pigment epithelium. The same necrotic tumour also gives the classic histological features of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes among viable cells and basophilic DNA staining of vessel walls.

question: 39 years old ptient with family hx of glaucoma presented to clinic as a routine checkup. Examination showed : IOP =16 mmgh , CDR = 0.8 and automated VF showed altitudinal defect. what is the most likely diagnosis :
explanation: Ocular hypertension is defined as a condition in which IOP is elevated above an arbitrary cutoff value, typically 21 mm Hg, in the absence of optic nerve, retinal nerve fiber layer, or visual field abnormalities. Controversy remains as to whether normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) represents a distinct disease entity or whether it is simply POAG developing in individuals with IOP within the statistically normal range. Glaucoma can develop at any level of IOP within the range ob- served in the general population NTG can be mimicked by conditions other than glaucoma. It is therefore essential to dis- tinguish glaucoma from other optic neuropathies (eg, optic nerve drusen, ischemic optic neuropathy) because appropriate therapy will differ (Table 7-2). Visual field defects in some of these conditions may appear similar to those seen with NTG and can even be progressive. The most common pattern of visual field loss in NAION is an altitudinal defect, but any pattern may be observed. Reference: AAO Glaucoma and NeuroOphtha Section

review.explanation: The patient has unmistakable glaucomatous damage, a cup-disc ratio of 0.8 with a matching field defect, while the intraocular pressure sits at 16 mmHg, and that combination defines normal-tension glaucoma. Ocular hypertension is the exact converse, a pressure above the statistical cut-off with a normal disc, normal nerve fibre layer and normal field, so it cannot apply to an eye with established damage. Classic POAG is diagnosed when the same damage occurs with pressures above the normal range. Diurnal phasing is worth doing, since a single 16 mmHg reading may miss peaks, and the family history is consistent with the genetic risk shared by the whole open-angle spectrum.
review.concern: An altitudinal field defect is a slightly atypical pattern for glaucoma and should prompt consideration of non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy and other compressive or ischaemic optic neuropathies before settling on normal-tension glaucoma; among the three options offered, however, only NTG fits.

question: Autofleuroscence will help to identify :
explanation: Although lipofuscin in the RPE is the main source of autofluorescence from the fundus, accumulation of fluorophore in the subretinal space is another important sig- nal source for the evaluation of some diseases, such as central serous chorioretinopathy. After the disease is present for a few months, the detachment becomes lighter and slightly more yellow in color, and the detachment also becomes hyperautofluorescent. Upon OCT imaging, an accumulation of material was found on the back surface of the retina in eyes with central serous chorioretinopathy with hyperautofluorescent detachments. It is thought that the photoreceptor outer segments are typically phagocytized and processed by the RPE, but if the retina has been physically elevated by fluid, the photoreceptors become separated from the RPE, thus impeding phagocytosis. This mechanism of disease pathophysiol- ogy may also be seen in vitelliform deposits in vitelliform macular dystrophy, adult vi- telliform lesions, the yellow material that builds up under chronic retinal detachments caused by optic pit maculopathy, and pockets of retained subretinal fluid after detach- ment surgery. Reference: AAO Retina Section

review.explanation: Fundus autofluorescence maps lipofuscin, whose dominant source is the retinal pigment epithelium, but that lipofuscin is generated by the RPE phagocytosing shed photoreceptor outer segments, so the signal reports on the health of the RPE-photoreceptor complex as a unit. In addition, subretinal accumulation of outer segment material is itself a fluorophore, which is why chronic central serous detachments become hyperautofluorescent. Reading autofluorescence therefore tells you about both partners, which is what option C says. The pure single-layer answer of RPE alone is the traditional teaching but understates what the modality is actually used for clinically, for example mapping geographic atrophy and its junctional hyperautofluorescent rim.
review.concern: If the examiner intended the narrower question of where the autofluorescent signal originates, RPE lipofuscin alone (option A) would be the expected answer. The source annotation marks C and the AAO passage supports the broader reading, so I have gone with C while noting that A is defensible.

Retroillumination uses light bounced back from the iris or fundus and is best for iris transillumination defects, lens opacities and epithelial or stromal irregularities silhouetted against a bright background. Diffuse illumination gives a broad low-magnification overview of the ocular surface and is useless for resolving a monolayer of cells.

question: Day 1 Post phaco with diffuse corneal edema and normal IOP. Cause ?

options.B: Collapse of the AC and IOL touch
options.C: Corneal decompensation due to fuch's dystrophy

explanation: Toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS) is an acute sterile postoperative inflammation. The symptoms and signs of TASS may mimic those of infectious endophthalmitis and include photophobia, severe reduction in visual acuity, corneal edema, and marked anterior chamber reaction, occasionally with hypopyon (Fig 11-17). However, TASS presents within 12 to 48 hours of surgery. potentially distinguishing features of TASS include diffuse, limbus-to-limbus corneal edema; anterior chamber fibrinous exudate; a dilated, irregular, or nonreactive pupil; and elevated IOP. The pathologic changes are limited to the anterior chamber. Pain is typically much milder than that experienced with an infection. Other causes of TASS include surgical glove residue or talc on instruments or IOLs; use of a denatured OVD; substitution of sterile water for balanced salt solution; intraocu- lar use of inappropriate irrigating solutions, antibiotics, or anesthetics; and inadvertent in- troduction of substances into the anterior chamber. Reference: AAO lens section

review.explanation: Diffuse limbus-to-limbus corneal oedema appearing on day one is the signature of toxic anterior segment syndrome, a sterile inflammation caused by something toxic entering the anterior chamber, whether contaminated irrigating solution, inadequately rinsed instruments, denatured viscoelastic, preservative or an incorrect intracameral drug concentration. The timing separates it from infectious endophthalmitis, which usually declares itself after two to seven days with far more pain. Fuchs dystrophy would have been evident preoperatively and typically produces central rather than limbus-to-limbus oedema with visible guttae. Anterior chamber collapse with lens-cornea touch causes focal, localised oedema at the contact zone, not diffuse whole-cornea oedema.

question: Intra-op PCR with dropped nucleus. Appropriate management:

options.B: Increase irrigation to rapidly aspirate the vitreous
options.C: Try to phacoemulsify the lens in anterior vitreous

explanation: If a small tear appears in the posterior capsule during aspiration of the cortex and the vitreous face remains intact, the surgeon can attempt to remove the residual cortex without expanding the tear. Using low-flow I/A and compartmentalizing the vitreous with an OVD If most of the nucleus remains and the capsular tear is large, further attempts at phacoemulsification should be abandoned. To extract the remaining nuclear fragments mechanically, the surgeon can enlarge the incision and remove the nucleus with a lens loop or spoon in a manner that minimizes vitreous traction and further damage to the capsule. Insertion of a second instrument or lens glide behind the nuclear remnant may help prevent the remnant from being dislocated into the vitreous. Alternatively, an OVD can be introduced posterior to the fragment in an effort to float it anteriorly, or the nucleus can be elevated into the anterior chamber with an instrument or nuclear spear. Retrieval of nuclear fragments from the deep vitreous is not recommended. If vitreous prolapse occurs, it is best to remove all vitreous from the anterior cham- ber during the initial surgery. Doing so will facilitate the removal of residual cortex and the subsequent placement of an IOL. In addition, a vitrectomy can reduce the chance of vitreoretinal traction or vitreous adherence to the IOL, the iris, or the incision. Vitreous loss during cataract surgery is associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment, cystoid macular edema, and endophthalmitis. The vitreous may be stained with unpreserved or washed triamcinolone for better visualization. A 2-port bimanual anterior vitrectomy can be per- formed with separate infusion and aspirating/cutting instruments inserted through new, properly sized limbal incisions (Fig 10-6A; Video 10-7). Alternatively, the aspiration/cut- ting instrument may be placed through a pars plana incision while irrigation is continued through the limbus Reference: AAO lens section

review.explanation: Once nucleus has descended into the vitreous cavity the anterior segment surgeon must not chase it. The correct move is to stop phacoemulsification, remove the prolapsed vitreous with a controlled bimanual anterior vitrectomy, and triamcinolone is injected precisely for this purpose, because it granulates onto vitreous strands and makes otherwise invisible vitreous visible so the vitrectomy can be complete. The eye is then closed, with an IOL placed if there is adequate support, and referred for pars plana lensectomy. Raising irrigation to aspirate vitreous is dangerous, because vitreous is not aspirable without traction and this invites giant retinal tear and detachment, and phacoemulsifying in the anterior vitreous transmits ultrasound energy and traction directly to the retina.

explanation: Peters anomaly type I is characterized by iridocorneal adhesions and a corneal opac- ity that is usually avascular and may be central, eccentric, or less commonly total. The syndrome is associated with mutations in PITX2, FOXC1, CYP1B1, PAX6, and other genes.
