Peters anomaly type II is presumed to be due to a developmental failure in separation of the invaginating lens vesicle from the overlying surface ectoderm. Mutations in the gene FOXE3 have been implicated in lens malformation in Peters anomaly type II. The same genetic mutation can cause Peters type I to occur in one eye and type II in the contralateral eye. High-frequency ultrasonography can be very useful in differentiating Peters types I and II, and sclerocornea. Glaucoma is present in 50% of Peters anomaly cases. Additional associated ocular abnormalities include microcornea, aniridia, retinal detachment, and PFV. The progno- sis for vision rehabilitation with corneal transplantation is better for patients with Peters anomaly type I than for those with type II Peters type I affects the cornea alone, type II shows both corneal and lens abnormalities. explanation: Angle recession is a common finding after blunt trauma and involves a tear between the longitudinal and circular muscle fibers of the ciliary body. Although angle recession is not necessarily associated with immediate IOP elevation and glaucoma, it is a sign of probable damage to the trabecular meshwork. Traumatic glaucoma is chronic and usually unilateral and may occur immediately after the ocular trauma or months to years later. It resembles POAG in presentation and clinical course but can be distinguished by its classic gonio- scopic findings widening of the ciliary body band; absent or torn iris processes; white, glistening scleral spur; irregular and dark pigmentation in the angle; PAS at the border of the recession

The associated findings are a widened ciliary body band, torn or absent iris processes, a white glistening scleral spur and peripheral anterior synechiae at the edges of the recession. The pressure rise may be immediate or appear months to years later, and the unilaterality is the key clue. Diabetes causes neovascular rather than recession glaucoma, penetrating injury produces a track and often epithelial downgrowth or a retained foreign body rather than a recessed angle, and viral disease (herpetic or Posner-Schlossman) raises pressure through trabeculitis with an open normal-appearing angle.

explanation: Bleb-related infection (Fig 13-16) is a potentially vision-threatening complication after trabeculectomy, occurring in 1.5%-6.0% of patients. Patients typically present with tearing, irritation, pain, and/or blurry vision. Risk factors for infection include untreated blepharitis, presence of an inferior bleb, bleb leak, and thin-walled blebs (which tend to occur with localized blebs). The use of MMC and 5-FU is also a risk factor, as these agents are associated with a higher incidence of thin-walled blebs and bleb leaks. One proposed classification scheme divides bleb-related infection into 3 stages, al- though these stages represent a continuum of infection: stage 1: erythema around the bleb, bleb infiltrate stage 2: anterior chamber inflammation stage 3: hypopyon and/or intravitreal involvement Stage 1 and stage 2 bleb-related infection (blebitis) can be treated with topical fluoroqui- nolones or fortified topical and subconjunctival antibiotics as needed. Stage 3, indicated by the presence of a hypopyon or intravitreal involvement (bleb- related endophthalmitis), warrants either a vitreous tap with injection of antibiotics or a vitrectomy. Patients with stage 1 and stage 2 bleb-related infection tend to fare well, while those with stage 3 tend to have poor visual outcomes. Reference: AAO Glaucoma Section

A B-scan is reserved for suspected posterior segment involvement, which a clear view of a normal fundus excludes.

review.explanation: A bluish, compressible periocular mass in a child whose size fluctuates is a lymphatic or venolymphatic malformation. Lymphatic malformations characteristically enlarge with upper respiratory infections, because the lymphoid tissue within them reacts, and can enlarge abruptly from intralesional haemorrhage producing so-called chocolate cysts. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the key differential and must be excluded, but it presents as a rapidly and relentlessly enlarging, usually superior and firm mass over days to weeks rather than a bluish lesion that waxes and wanes, and it does not fluctuate with position or intercurrent illness.
review.concern: The phrase increasing with cold is almost certainly a garbled recall; the meaningful clinical triggers are crying or Valsalva (which distend an orbital varix or venous malformation) and upper respiratory infection (which enlarges a lymphatic malformation). With only two options offered, the lymphatic malformation is the answer.

question: closing her eyes , what other features ?
explanation: Myasthenia gravis

review.explanation: This is ocular myasthenia gravis, and its defining characteristic is fatigability, so sustained upgaze for a minute progressively worsens the ptosis while a period of eye closure or rest improves it, which is the basis of the rest test. Cooling improves myasthenic ptosis rather than worsening it, which is exactly why the ice-pack test is a useful bedside manoeuvre, so option B is inverted. Lid lag on downgaze, von Graefe sign, belongs to thyroid eye disease, where the lid retraction reflects sympathetic overactivity and levator-superior rectus fibrosis. Look also for a Cogan lid twitch and for variable, pupil-sparing diplopia in any pattern.
review.concern: The stem is truncated in the recall, but the answer options and the source annotation make the underlying diagnosis of myasthenia gravis unambiguous.

question: pic of 3 year old child with superotemoral mass ( looks dermoid cyst ) What thing to be cautious about during sx ?

review.explanation: A dermoid cyst is lined by keratinising epithelium and filled with keratin, sebaceous material and hair, all of which are intensely inflammatory once outside the capsule, so intraoperative rupture provokes a granulomatous foreign body reaction with prolonged inflammation, scarring, fistula formation and a high recurrence rate. The surgical principle is therefore complete excision of the cyst with its capsule intact, dissecting circumferentially without grasping the wall in a way that tears it. Haemorrhage is not a particular hazard of a superficial superotemporal dermoid, and levator injury relates to lid surgery rather than to a lesion sitting at the frontozygomatic suture, although a deeper dumbbell lesion extending through bone should be identified on imaging beforehand.

question: 22 IOP means:
explanation: lOP has a non-Gaussian distribution with a skew toward higher pressures, especially in individuals older than 40 years .The value 21 mm Hg (greater than 2 standard deviations above the mean) was traditionally used both to separate normal and abnormal pressures and to define which patients required ocular hypotensive therapy.

review.explanation: The population mean intraocular pressure is about 15.5 mmHg with a standard deviation of about 2.6, so the traditional cut-off of 21 mmHg sits roughly two standard deviations above the mean, and 22 mmHg is therefore above the two standard deviation mark. Option A is wrong because the distribution of intraocular pressure is not Gaussian: it is skewed toward higher values, particularly after the age of 40, which is exactly why a purely statistical cut-off is a poor disease definition. Option C is wrong because the great majority of people sit well below 21 mmHg. The clinical lesson is that 22 mmHg is a statistical outlier, not a diagnosis, and glaucoma is defined by optic nerve and field damage rather than by a pressure number.

question: 3 days post Trabeculectomy with flat bleb and IOP 40 mmhg with pain and shallow AC and patent PI and normal fundus. cause:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: The combination that defines aqueous misdirection, or malignant glaucoma, is a shallow or flat anterior chamber with a high intraocular pressure, a flat bleb, a patent peripheral iridotomy and no choroidal detachment or suprachoroidal haemorrhage on fundus examination. Aqueous is being diverted posteriorly into or behind the vitreous, pushing the whole lens-iris diaphragm forward. A bleb leak is excluded on two counts: it produces hypotony rather than a pressure of 40, and it would not give a flat bleb with a hard eye. The patent iridotomy is what excludes pupillary block, and the normal fundus is what excludes suprachoroidal haemorrhage, which would also give a shallow chamber with a high pressure and severe pain.

question: day 1 post phaco with 700 micron corneal thickness, and 24 IOP ... measurement will be:
explanation: Corneal thickness has been shown to affect IOP readings, with thin corneas resulting in a falsely low IOP, and thick corneas resulting in a falsely high IOP.

review.explanation: Goldmann applanation was calibrated for a central corneal thickness of about 520 microns, and the Imbert-Fick assumptions break down as thickness departs from that value: a thicker cornea resists flattening and so overestimates the true pressure, while a thin cornea underestimates it. At 700 microns the reading of 24 mmHg is therefore likely to be higher than the true intraocular pressure, and the finding should be interpreted rather than treated reflexively. Applying a mucolytic such as N-acetylcysteine does nothing to change the biomechanics of measurement and is not a tonometry technique.
review.concern: There is an important caveat the resident should know. The simple thickness rule applies to intrinsically thick, structurally normal corneas. An acutely oedematous cornea, as on day one after phacoemulsification, is thickened by fluid in a softened, less rigid stroma, and applanation over an oedematous cornea is classically said to underestimate the true pressure. So while option A is the intended answer and the thickness rule is what is being tested, the real day-one reading in this eye may be less predictable than the rule suggests.

question: received multiple subtenon steroid which anesthesia is C/I in phaco?(same Q in provision)

review.explanation: Repeated sub-Tenon depot steroid injections fibrose the sub-Tenon and episcleral planes and can leave focal scleral thinning at the injection site. A peribulbar block depends on a large volume of anaesthetic diffusing from the extraconal space through those tissue planes to reach the muscle cone, so scarring both impairs the spread and makes the block unreliable, while needle placement adjacent to a thinned sclera raises the risk of globe perforation. In an eye with a scarred orbit the safest choice is topical anaesthesia with intracameral lidocaine, which avoids any needle near the globe altogether.
review.concern: This item is a poor recall and I am not confident in the keyed answer. The technique most obviously compromised by repeated sub-Tenon injections is a sub-Tenon (parabulbar) block itself, and that option is not offered. Nothing about prior sub-Tenon steroid is a recognised absolute contraindication to a peribulbar block over a retrobulbar one, so I would treat this question as unreliable and simply remember the safe principle that a scarred orbit favours topical and intracameral anaesthesia.

question: 70 Yrs Old Immunocompetent with floaters, vitreous cells, peripheral vasculitis and large retinitis (ARN picture):

review.explanation: Acute retinal necrosis is a herpetic necrotising retinitis caused by varicella zoster virus or herpes simplex, and it is defined by peripheral confluent full-thickness retinal necrosis, occlusive arteritis and prominent vitritis and anterior chamber inflammation in an immunocompetent host, exactly as described. CMV retinitis is the disease of the profoundly immunosuppressed and characteristically produces minimal vitritis with an indolent granular or haemorrhagic brushfire border. Toxoplasmosis gives a focal creamy retinochoroiditis, usually adjacent to an old pigmented scar, rather than large circumferential peripheral necrosis. Behcet disease produces occlusive retinal vasculitis with recurrent hypopyon uveitis and systemic oral and genital ulceration, not necrotising retinitis of this pattern. Treatment is urgent systemic antiviral therapy with consideration of intravitreal antiviral and prophylactic attention to the fellow eye.

question: Which subtype of BCC has the Highest recurrence if not completely removed:
explanation: Histologic types of BCC at higher risk for recurrence include morpheaform (sclerotic), micronodular, infiltrative, and superficial (multicentric).

review.explanation: Morpheaform, also called sclerosing, basal cell carcinoma spreads as thin infiltrative strands within a dense fibrous stroma, so its true extent is far greater than its clinically visible margin and it is the subtype most likely to recur after incomplete excision. Micronodular, infiltrative and superficial multicentric subtypes share this risk. Nodular basal cell carcinoma is well demarcated with a pearly rolled edge and is the most common and most easily excised subtype. Pigmented basal cell carcinoma is a nodular variant with melanin and behaves like the nodular type. The practical consequence is that morpheaform lesions, and any lesion at the medial canthus, are best managed with Mohs micrographic surgery or careful frozen section margin control.

question: Treatment of basal cell carcinoma:

options.A: surgical excision with frozen section and free margin

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Complete surgical excision with histological margin control, whether by Mohs micrographic surgery or by excision with frozen section monitoring of the margins, is the treatment of choice for eyelid basal cell carcinoma and gives the highest cure rate with the least sacrifice of normal lid tissue. Topical antimetabolites such as 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod have a limited role in superficial non-eyelid lesions and cannot be relied on for margin clearance or for periocular disease. Radiotherapy, whether external beam or brachytherapy, is reserved for patients unfit for surgery or for adjuvant use in perineural or incompletely excised disease, and it carries real ocular surface, lacrimal and cataractogenic toxicity. Option D is not a meaningful description of any radiotherapy technique.

question: Seen in bruchs membrane of Angoid streak:
explanation: Histopathologic studies have shown extensive calcification and thickening of Bruch's membrane and the intervening interstitial space between capillaries. Histopathologic break's in Bruch's membrane correspond to the clinical location of angioid streaks. Ingrowth of fibrovascular tissue may occur from the choroid into the sub retinal pigment epithelial space, Eye Wiki

review.explanation: Angioid streaks are dehiscences in a Bruch membrane that has become thickened, brittle and calcified, and it is calcium deposition that makes the membrane crack in the radiating pattern seen around the disc. The systemic associations follow the same logic of abnormal elastic tissue and mineralisation, chiefly pseudoxanthoma elasticum, and also Paget disease, the haemoglobinopathies including sickle cell disease, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Lipid accumulation in Bruch membrane is a feature of ageing and age-related macular degeneration rather than of angioid streaks, and iron deposition belongs to siderosis. Patients need counselling about the risk of choroidal neovascularisation growing through the breaks and about the risk of choroidal rupture from even minor blunt trauma.

question: optic nerve drusen is associated with:
explanation: Eyewiki: They can be associated with retinitis pigmentosa, angioid streaks, Usher syndrome, Noonan syndrome and Alagille syndrome.

review.explanation: Optic nerve head drusen are calcified hyaline bodies within a crowded, small-scleral-canal disc, and they are described in association with retinitis pigmentosa, angioid streaks and pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Usher syndrome, Noonan syndrome and Alagille syndrome. Giant cell arteritis is not an association; it causes arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy with chalky pallid disc swelling. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension causes genuine papilloedema, and the clinically important relationship is one of confusion rather than association, because buried drusen produce pseudopapilloedema that is mistaken for papilloedema. The distinguishing features are absent disc hyperaemia, no obscuration of vessels at the disc margin, anomalous vessel branching, and autofluorescence, B-scan or OCT demonstrating the drusen.

question: Pic of a child with high IOP and no bufthalmus. What gene is affected?
explanation: The prevalence is higher in cultures with consanguinity, particularly those with a high carrier rate of CYP1B1 gene (GLC3A locus on chromosome 2p21). There appears to be no association with adult primary open-angle glaucoma. Eye Wiki

review.explanation: The explicit statement that there is no buphthalmos is the discriminator in this stem. The infant eye is distensible, so glaucoma presenting before roughly three years of age enlarges the globe and cornea and gives buphthalmos with Haab striae, and that entity is primary congenital glaucoma, linked to CYP1B1 at the GLC3A locus. Once the sclera has stiffened, glaucoma in an older child raises pressure without enlarging the eye, and that juvenile open-angle glaucoma is the phenotype classically caused by myocilin (MYOC, GLC1A) mutations, inherited autosomal dominantly and often with very high pressures needing early surgery. OPTN mutations are associated with normal-tension glaucoma in adults, and LOXL1 with exfoliation syndrome, so neither fits a child.
review.concern: I disagree with the keyed answer of CYP1B1 on the basis of the words no buphthalmos, which point to juvenile rather than congenital onset and therefore to myocilin. I cannot see the photograph, and this is the caveat: if the image showed an infant with a hazy enlarged cornea or Haab striae, then primary congenital glaucoma and CYP1B1 would be correct and the source key would stand. CYP1B1 has also been reported in some juvenile-onset cases in consanguineous populations, so the two are not entirely exclusive.

question: Pic of Multiple large Soft drusen + OCT:
explanation: Classification Early ARMD: Defined by the presence of numerous small (<63 microns, "hard") or intermediate (≥63 microns but <125 microns, "soft") drusen. Note: Small drusen are frequently seen in those 50 and older, and can represent an epiphenomenon of aging (therefore, intermediate drusen are more specific for ARMD Intermediate ARMD: Macular disease characterized by either extensive drusen of small or intermediate size, or any drusen of large size (≥125 microns). Advanced ARMD: Defined by the presence of either geographic atrophy or choroidal neovascular membrane (along with its sequelae, such as subretinal or sub-RPE hemorrhage or serous fluid, and subretinal fibrosis). 29 months. • Eye Wiki

review.explanation: Using the AREDS classification, any drusen of large size, meaning 125 microns or more which is roughly the width of a retinal vein at the disc margin, or extensive intermediate drusen, defines intermediate age-related macular degeneration. Early disease is defined by small hard drusen under 63 microns or a few intermediate drusen with no large ones. Advanced disease requires either geographic atrophy involving the fovea or neovascular disease with its sequelae of subretinal fluid, haemorrhage or fibrosis, none of which is described here. The classification matters practically, because it is at the intermediate stage with large drusen that AREDS2 supplementation is indicated and home Amsler monitoring should be taught.

question: FFA of Indian: with VH & periphral NV (Eale'. Which test?

review.explanation: Eales disease is an idiopathic occlusive periphlebitis of young adult males, classically from the Indian subcontinent, presenting with peripheral non-perfusion, neovascularisation and recurrent vitreous haemorrhage, and it is strongly associated with hypersensitivity to tuberculoprotein, so tuberculin skin testing is characteristically positive and is the investigation asked for. The diagnosis remains one of exclusion, and the relevant workup also includes a chest radiograph and an interferon gamma release assay. Syphilis serology, whether the non-treponemal VDRL or the treponemal FTA-ABS, screens for a different mimic and is reasonable in a uveitis workup generally, but neither is the test tied to Eales disease. Management is laser photocoagulation to the ischaemic peripheral retina, with vitrectomy for non-clearing haemorrhage.

question: Moreen ulcer:

explanation: Systemic immunosuppression using cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, or methotrexate can be attempted if conjunctival resection yields no improvement . Interferon alpha 2b has been used in patients who had hepatitis C and concomitant Mooren's ulceration. In more aggressive cases, oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine A, and methotrexate have also been used with some success Eye Wiki

review.explanation: Mooren ulcer occurs in two forms: a limited, unilateral, relatively indolent type in older patients, and an aggressive, bilateral, relentlessly progressive type in younger patients, so option A reverses the association. A well-recognised subset is associated with hepatitis C, and in those patients treating the underlying viral infection with interferon alfa-2b, with or without ribavirin, can produce dramatic healing of the ulcer, which makes B correct. The third stem fragment about progression toward the sclera is also wrong: sparing of the sclera is one of the features that separates Mooren ulcer from the peripheral ulcerative keratitis of systemic vasculitis, and Mooren spreads circumferentially and then centrally with an undermined leading edge.

question: Large descemts detachment Management:
explanation: Eyewiki: Transcorneal interrupted suturing using a 10/00 monofilament Nylon suture has been described, frequently associated with intracameral injection of air/gas.

review.explanation: The aim in Descemet membrane detachment is to reappose the membrane to the posterior stroma, normally achieved by descemetopexy with an air or gas bubble such as SF6 or C3F8. For a large, planar or chronic detachment that will not tamponade with gas alone, transcorneal full-thickness 10-0 monofilament nylon sutures are placed to mechanically press the membrane back, usually combined with an intracameral air or gas fill, so A is the intended answer. Silicone oil in the anterior chamber has no role here and would risk endothelial damage and pressure problems, and deliberately leaving a large bolus of viscoelastic is actively harmful because it keeps the membrane away from the stroma and causes an intraocular pressure spike.

question: Europian society recommendation to prevent post-op endophthalmitis post phaco:
explanation: Intracameral injection of cefuroxime during phacoemulsification is considered effective in preventing endophthalmitis.

review.explanation: The ESCRS multicentre endophthalmitis study demonstrated an approximately fivefold reduction in postoperative endophthalmitis with intracameral cefuroxime 1 mg in 0.1 mL given at the end of phacoemulsification, and this is the European recommendation. Perioperative topical fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin did not show a statistically significant independent protective effect in that trial and is adjunctive at best. Vancomycin in the irrigating bottle is specifically not recommended: the delivered dose is unreliable, it promotes resistance to a last-line antistaphylococcal agent, and it has been linked to haemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis.

question: CIN characteristic:

options.A: Dysplasia : they classify CIN into mild moderate severe based on degree of dysplasia

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia is by definition a dysplastic lesion of the surface epithelium, graded mild, moderate or severe according to how much of the epithelial thickness is occupied by dysplastic cells, becoming carcinoma in situ when full thickness, so dysplasia is the defining and grading characteristic. Loss of normal maturation, nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitoses and loss of goblet cells accompany it, while the epithelial basement membrane stays intact, which is what separates CIN from invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Acanthosis, hyperkeratosis seen clinically as leukoplakia, and epithelial hyperplasia are frequently present but are non-specific reactive changes that also occur in benign lesions such as pterygium or papilloma, so none of them defines the lesion.

question: Which one is a Main. Branch of facial nerve

review.explanation: The facial nerve emerges from the parotid gland as five main branches: temporal (frontal), zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical, so zygomatic is the only unambiguously correct main branch listed. The zygomaticofacial and infraorbital branches are sensory branches of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, not of cranial nerve VII, which is the trap in this item. Temporal is a genuine main branch, but temporo-parietal is not the accepted anatomical name and conflates the nerve with the temporoparietal fascia, so zygomatic remains the best answer.

question: Rounding of medial canthus:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Rounding or blunting of the normally sharp medial canthal angle is the classic sign that the medial canthal tendon has been avulsed or disinserted, typically with a canalicular laceration or a naso-orbito-ethmoid injury, and it is usually accompanied by traumatic telecanthus and lateral displacement of the punctum. A medial wall blowout fracture on its own does not detach the tendon and presents instead with enophthalmos, orbital emphysema or restricted abduction. A tumour or an acute dacryocystitis produces a mass or an inflamed swelling below the medial canthal tendon but leaves the canthal angle itself anatomically intact.

review.explanation: The Branch Vein Occlusion Study set the treatment threshold for macular oedema after BRVO as visual acuity of 20/40 or worse persisting for at least 3 months, with intraretinal haemorrhage cleared enough to permit angiography and grid laser, which is exactly option A. A specific retinal thickness value, distance from the FAZ, or the presence of hard exudates were not BVOS criteria; five disc diameters of non-perfusion is the BVOS threshold for watching for neovascularisation, not for treating oedema, so D is a deliberate near-miss. question: year-old patient underwent complicated cataract and DSAEK. 3 months later VA is not improved. Which of the following is the best to maximize vision improvement?
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document. potential acuity estimation; computerized corneal topography; anterior segment OCT; trial of gas permeable contact lens the most site of resistance in aqueous flow: Juxtacanalicular; uveal meshwork; corneosclearal; schlemm canal

review.explanation: After a complicated cataract extraction, pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema is the commonest treatable reason for vision failing to improve once the cornea has cleared, and it is easily confirmed on macular OCT and treated with topical NSAID plus corticosteroid, escalating to sub-Tenon or intravitreal steroid. PTK addresses anterior stromal irregularity and would do nothing for an endothelial or macular problem, and would in fact induce a hyperopic shift. Cultured endothelial cell therapy is investigational rather than a standard clinical option. Repeat DSAEK is indicated only if the graft has actually failed or dislocated, which this stem does not state, so treating the macula is the intervention most likely to gain vision.
